Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication:
A Review
Lei Jin<sup>1</sup>  · Zhao‑Yun Wang<sup>2</sup> · Fang‑Zu Yang<sup>3</sup>
Received: 1 February 2025 / Accepted: 12 July 2025 / Published online: 7 August 2025
© The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society 2025
Abstract
Electroplating is a core technology in high-end chip manufacturing, with its technical challenges centered on achieving void-
free filling of metal coatings within micro- and nanoscale trenches and vias. Copper, the current mainstream interconnect
material, can no longer meet the performance and reliability demands posed by the continuous reduction in interconnect
dimensions. In contrast, cobalt ofers superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, making it a promising
next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of cobalt interconnect
technology in chip manufacturing. It examines the electrochemical behavior and interactions of cobalt ions, boric acid, and
additives, summarizing the cobalt filling efects and associated mechanism models under diferent process compositions. The
discussion also highlights advanced in situ electrochemical characterization technologies to investigate the synergistic and
antagonistic efects of various plating bath components, the influence of pH, temperature, and additives on cobalt nuclea-
tion and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures.
Furthermore, the paper explores annealing treatments for cobalt coatings, emphasizing their role in optimizing performance.

Cobalt interconnects still use classical damascene pro-
cess. As shown in Fig. 4, after the via or trench is etched,

ricated by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and atomic

to be further explored.

troplating, the role of each component, and the mechanism
of superfilling are reviewed, and the basic research and tech-

Additives and Superfilling Mechanism
Metal cobalt is an iron group element, so the additives suit-
able for electroplating of iron group metals can be used for
cobalt electroplating. Alkynol/enol compounds (including
sulfonated compounds) are typical additives for cobalt elec-
trodeposition. The molecular structure is shown in Fig. 8.
However, to date, there are almost no reports on the use

also some mechanisms that do not limit the kinds of addi-

changes directly afected the concentration of hydroxide
ions involved in the formation of intermediates,

thereby increasing the reaction paths, changing the thermo-
dynamics of cobalt electrodeposition, and adjusting the rate
of cobalt electrodeposition. They confirmed that there was
a concentration gradient of hydrogen ions in the via (high
concentration at the mouth of via), and the current eficiency
of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom of the via was four
times higher than that at the mouth by using cyclic voltam-

Another mechanism that is not afected by the types of addi-

process, a large amount of atomic hydrogen accumulates

ratio, and the inhibitor at the bottom of via is continuously
protonated and loses the ability to inhibit the electro-reduc-
tion of cobalt ions. A schematic of the HID mechanism is
presented in Fig. 12. According to the principles described
in this mechanism, any additive that undergoes a transition
between an inactive state and active state under the influence
of hydrogen ions can control and achieve the cobalt bottom-
up superfilling.

fusion. However, dye molecules are often unstable and are

Electro‑reduction
Cobalt ion is a divalent metal ion. In the inherent impression,
divalent cobalt is directly electro-reduced to metal cobalt,
and the chemical formula is:
\mathrm { C o ^ { 2 + } } \ + 2 \mathrm { e } = \mathrm { C o ( s ) . } ^ { 6 1 , 6 2 }
How-
ever, divalent cobalt ions, like iron group elements, need to
go through an intermediate state for electro-reduction.<sup>63–68</sup>
The electro-reduction reaction of cobalt ions proceeds in a
continuous one-electron transfer step through the adsorbed
cobalt hydroxide intermediate, and the corresponding
chemical formulae are shown below.<sup>56</sup> It is worth noting
that Rigsby et al.<sup>56</sup> confirmed that the rate of cobalt electro-
reduction varies depending on the concentration of hydrox-
ide ions.
\mathrm{Co} ^ {2 +} + \mathrm{OH} ^ {-} = \left(\mathrm{CoOH} ^ {+}\right) _ {\mathrm{ads}}\tag{1}
\left(\mathrm{CoOH} ^ {+}\right) _ {\mathrm{ads}} + \mathrm{e} = (\mathrm{CoOH}) _ {\mathrm{ads}}\tag{2}
(\mathrm{CoOH}) _ {\mathrm{ads}} + \mathrm{e} = \mathrm{Co(s)} + \mathrm{OH} ^ {-}\tag{3}
Some researchers have diferent views on the electro-
reduction of cobalt ion. Santos et al.<sup>69</sup> deemed that the cobalt
ions combine with the hydroxide to form cobalt hydrox-
ide, which is a competitive reaction with the cobalt ions
being directly electro-reduced to metal cobalt. The formed
cobalt hydroxide is adsorbed on the electrode surface, and
obtains two electrons at a relatively negative potential to be
electro-reduced to metal cobalt. The corresponding chemi-
cal formulae are:
\mathrm{Co} ^ {2 +} + 2 \mathrm{OH} ^ {-} = \left(\mathrm{Co} (\mathrm{OH}) _ {2}\right) _ {\mathrm{ads}}\tag{4}
\left(\mathrm{Co} (\mathrm{OH}) _ {2}\right) _ {\mathrm{ads}} + 2 \mathrm{e} = \mathrm{Co} (\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{OH} ^ {-}\tag{5}
Nucleation and Growth
The nucleation and growth process of cobalt interconnect
wires has a huge impact on their stability and resistivity.
Pagnanelli et al.<sup>70</sup> found that increasing the overpotential of
cobalt electrodeposition will increase the number of active
sites on the surface, resulting in an increase in the density
of cobalt nuclei and a significant decrease in grain size.
Mehmood et al.<sup>71</sup> confirmed that the overpotential of cobalt
electrodeposition is closely related to its growth structure.
High overpotential is conducive to the formation of face-
centered cubic cobalt clusters with a small core radius. In
addition, pH has an efect on the nucleation of micron-scale
cobalt, but has no efect on the nucleation of nanoscale
cobalt.<sup>72</sup> Mukhtar et al.<sup>73</sup> showed that the concentration of
cobalt ion has a significant efect on its nucleation. When
the concentration is low, the cobalt nucleus is larger and the
structure is hexagonal close-packed. As the concentration is
high, the cobalt nucleus is smaller and the structure is face-
centered cubic. A schematic is shown in Fig. 13.
The presence of additives can also afect the nucleation
behavior of cobalt. Hu et al.<sup>34</sup> reported the nucleation and
growth process of cobalt under the action of diferent addi-
tives (DMG, CHD). As shown in Fig. 14, there was a two-
step nucleation process on the electrode surface, including
electro-reduction of cobalt coordination ions (formed by
additives and cobalt ions) and direct electro-reduction of
cobalt ions. Furthermore, Hu et al.<sup>74</sup> also discovered that
the threshold potential for nucleation decreased upon the
increase of furil dioxime concentration, and the deposition
was found to follow the progressive nucleation behavior for
almost all cases.
Electrochemical Oscillation
The phenomenon that an autocatalytic reaction causes a
positive feedback loop is regard as electrochemical oscil-
lation.<sup>75–78</sup> The self-adsorption/desorption, decomposition
and competitive adsorption of additives on the electrode
surface may change the kinetic mechanism of metal ion
electro-reduction, resulting in electrochemical oscillation,
and periodic changes in current or potential within a certain
range.<sup>78–81</sup> Numerous studies on electrochemical oscillation
for copper interconnects have been reported,<sup>82–85</sup> but, to the
best of our knowledge, only one report on the electrochemi-
cal oscillation of cobalt interconnects has been published.
Hu et al. <sup>86</sup> reported that 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate
(MPS) can lead to an electrochemical oscillation. The main
positive feedback loops resulting in oscillation are auto-
catalytic accumulation and dissolution of cobalt hydroxide,
which are triggered by the potential-dependent adsorption
and desorption of the Co-MPS complex. Figure 15 shows the
potential oscillation phenomen0n and mechanism of cobalt.
Coordination
Additive molecules can coordinate metal ions on the elec-
trode surface, thereby changing the electrode process kinet-
ics of metal deposition. For example, in copper intercon-
nects, MPS can coordinate with copper and chloride ions to
form a complex, thereby accelerating copper electrodeposi-
tion.<sup>87,88</sup> Polyethylene glycol can also coordinate with cop-
per and chloride ions to form a complex to inhibit copper
electrodeposition,
<sup>89,90</sup> while cobalt ions can also coordi-
nate with additives during electro-reduction. Li et  al.<sup>31</sup>
showed that a coordination interaction is formed between
the opened nitrogenous heterocyclic ring in NBT and cobalt
ions, as the cobalt ions move toward the electrode surface.

Electrochemical Oscillation
The phenomenon that an autocatalytic reaction causes a
positive feedback loop is regard as electrochemical oscil-
lation.<sup>75–78</sup> The self-adsorption/desorption, decomposition
and competitive adsorption of additives on the electrode
surface may change the kinetic mechanism of metal ion
electro-reduction, resulting in electrochemical oscillation,
and periodic changes in current or potential within a certain
range.<sup>78–81</sup> Numerous studies on electrochemical oscillation

best of our knowledge, only one report on the electrochemi-
cal oscillation of cobalt interconnects has been published.
Hu et al. <sup>86</sup> reported that 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate

positive feedback loops resulting in oscillation are auto-
catalytic accumulation and dissolution of cobalt hydroxide,
which are triggered by the potential-dependent adsorption
and desorption of the Co-MPS complex. Figure 15 shows the
potential oscillation phenomen0n and mechanism of cobalt.
Coordination
Additive molecules can coordinate metal ions on the elec-

form a complex, thereby accelerating copper electrodeposi-
tion.<sup>87,88</sup> Polyethylene glycol can also coordinate with cop-
per and chloride ions to form a complex to inhibit copper
electrodeposition,

nate with additives during electro-reduction. Li et  al.<sup>31</sup>
showed that a coordination interaction is formed between
the opened nitrogenous heterocyclic ring in NBT and cobalt
ions, as the cobalt ions move toward the electrode surface.

Potential Future Direction
At present, the study of cobalt electroplating often obtains
average information of various thermodynamics and kinet-
ics of the electrode/solution interface and electrode surface
processes at the macrolevel by using classical electrochemi-
cal research methods and theoretical calculations. However,
classical electrochemical research methods find it dificult
to identify the characteristics of electrode reaction inter-
mediates and products, and cannot provide mechanism
information at the microscopic and molecular levels. Some
advanced in situ characterization methods are used in cop-
per electroplating
.<sup>96–99</sup> Therefore, advanced electrochemical
in situ research methods should be used in the future. In
addition, annealing treatment of cobalt coatings is also a
future research direction.
1. Electrochemical in situ infrared spectroscopy can reveal
the adsorption, orientation, bonding, dissociation, and
other behaviors of species at the electrode/electrolyte
interface, as well as the real-time changes of various
species during the electrochemical reaction.<sup>90,100–102</sup>
Since the Raman signal of water molecules is very
weak, electrochemical in situ surface-enhanced Raman
spectroscopy has high sensitivity, high signal-to-noise
ratio and spatial resolution, which is conducive to study-
ing the molecular mechanism of additives.<sup>103–105</sup> At the
same time, Raman spectroscopy has been combined
with digital imaging technology to develop a Raman
mapping technology, which can obtain the spatial dis-
tribution information of specific spectral characteristics
of Raman-active molecules.<sup>106,107</sup>
2. The nucleation and growth process of cobalt electro-
crystallization determines the quality and performance
of the cobalt coating.<sup>108</sup> Since the cobalt nucleation and
growth process is very rapid, the crystal nuclei grown
at the solid/liquid interface are submicron/nanoscale,
which brings certain difficulties to in  situ research.
In situ transmission electron microscopy or in situ scan-
ning electron microscopy) has high spatial resolution
and are the most intuitive and eficient research method
for studying nucleation and growth.<sup>109–111</sup> In situ obser-
vation, recording the nucleation and growth behavior of
the initial stage of metal deposition, and studying the
influence of additives on the cobalt nucleation process
and growth, can provide theoretical guidance and tech-
nical support for electroplating, especially chip electro-
plating.
3. X-ray difraction (XRD) is an efective means of ana-
lyzing the structure of the coating, and can obtain the
properties of the coating, such as atomic arrangement,
preferred crystal orientation, grain size, and micro-
stress.<sup>112,113</sup>
These properties determine the physical
properties of the interconnects, such as conductivity,
thermal conductivity, and ductility, and thus determine
the quality of the interconnects. Electrochemical in situ
XRD technology can monitor the dynamic evolution
of coating composition, crystal face, and structure in
real time, and study the mechanism of the influence of
plating solution composition on the properties of the
coating. It is crucial to reveal the structure–activity rela-
tionship between the structure and physical properties
of the coating and to establish an interconnect quality
evaluation mechanism.
4. The introduction of impurity atoms afects the grain
structure and preferred orientation of cobalt, and its
redistribution and segregation in the coating will also
afect the change of resistance.<sup>114,115</sup> Like copper elec-
troplating, the electroplated cobalt also needs to be
annealed and recrystallized to allow the impurities in
the coating to escape and thus improve its conductivity.

increasingly unable to meet the required performance and
safety standards. Cobalt, with its superior electrical prop-
erties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, is emerging as a
promising next-generation interconnect material to replace
copper. Although there have been reports on cobalt elec-
troplating, current research has primarily focused on the
electrochemical behavior of cobalt ions and additives, the
role of additives, and the filling efects in trenches and vias,
along with proposed filling mechanisms. However, several
key aspects remain insuficiently explored. These include
the specific actions and synergistic/antagonistic interac-
tions of components such as boric acid and additives in the
plating bath, the mechanisms by which pH, temperature,
and individual bath components influence cobalt nucleation
and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes
during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures.
